title: Consider static factory methods instead of constructors
concept: Instead of always exposing a public constructor, a class can provide a static method that returns an instance. This gives the method a descriptive name, lets it return a cached or subtype instance instead of always creating a new object, and doesn't force every instance into an identical construction pattern.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: You're designing a class where instances are expensive to create and often reused — constructor or factory?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: Static factory — it lets you cache and return existing instances instead of allocating a new one every time, and gives the method a descriptive name instead of an opaque new call.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: You're writing a simple data class meant to be subclassed by consumers of your library — public constructor or static-factory-only?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Public (or protected) constructor. A class with only private constructors and static factories can't be subclassed, so this is a real case where static factories are the wrong choice.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of relying only on static factory methods instead of public constructors?
options: They cannot be given descriptive names
Classes without public/protected constructors cannot be subclassed
They always create a new object on every call
They cannot return cached instances

quiz.question: Which of the following is an advantage static factory methods have over constructors?
options: They can return an instance of a subtype chosen at runtime
They are required to always return a new instance
They must have the same name as the class
They cannot be overloaded

quiz.question: Boolean.valueOf(boolean) is an example of which static factory benefit?
options: Returning a cached instance instead of always allocating a new one
Enforcing subclassing
Guaranteeing thread creation
Avoiding the need for any constructor at all

quiz.question: What is a common naming convention for a static factory that always returns a new instance distinct from its argument's type?
options: getInstance
valueOf
newInstance / create
build

quiz.question: Why can static factory methods be harder to discover in API documentation compared to constructors?
options: They're not listed in Javadoc at all
They don't stand out the way constructors do, since they look like any other static method
They must be private
Java doesn't allow Javadoc comments on static methods

interview_questions.question: Why might you choose a static factory method over a public constructor in Java?
interview_questions.model_answer: Static factories can have descriptive names, return cached or existing instances instead of always allocating new ones, and can return a subtype chosen at runtime — none of which a constructor can do.

interview_questions.question: Here's a class with only a public constructor that's called thousands of times per second with mostly repeated argument values. What would you change?
interview_questions.model_answer: Replace the public constructor with a private one plus a static factory method that caches and returns common instances, avoiding redundant allocation.

interview_questions.question: What's a downside of making all your constructors private and only exposing static factories?
interview_questions.model_answer: The class can no longer be subclassed by consumers, since subclassing requires a public or protected constructor — this can be a real limitation for extensible library classes.

interview_questions.question: How does Optional.of() in the Java standard library demonstrate the static factory pattern?
interview_questions.model_answer: Optional.of() gives a clear, descriptive name to construction (versus an opaque new Optional(...)), and the API intentionally hides the constructor entirely, exposing only factories like of, empty, and ofNullable.
